Aims: The aim of present study was to investigate the effects of isosteviol on hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia
in rats fed with high-fat emulsion (HFE).
Main methods: Hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia in rats was induced by daily ingestion of HFE for 14 days. Isosteviol (0.2, 1.0, or 5.0 mg/kg/day) was orally administered for 7 days, with rosiglitazone maleate (5.0 mg/kg/
day) used as the positive control. The levels of fasting serum glucose (FSG), fasting serum insulin (FSI), total
cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG), high density lipoprotein (HDL), and low density lipoprotein (LDL) in serum
were assayed. Intravenous glucose tolerance test (IVGTT) was performed with serum glucose and insulin levels
monitored. The effect of the supplement of palmitate in HFE on the activity of isosteviol was investigated. Ultrastructural changes in islet β-cells and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α (PPARα) mRNA expression
proﬁle were determined.
Key ﬁndings: FSG, FSI, TC and LDL levels and insulin resistance index (IRI) were decreased and HDL level was
increased by all doses of isosteviol. During IVGTT, serum glucose levels were decreased by isosteviol and no
signiﬁcant differences were observed in insulin release between isosteviol-treated and control groups. The
effects of isosteviol were attenuated by palmitate. Damage to pancreatic islet cells was partially attenuated,
and expression proﬁle of hepatic PPARα mRNA was enhanced by isosteviol.
Signiﬁcance: Antihyperglycemic effects of isosteviol could enhance utilization of glucose in the periphery
and reduce β-cell damage induced by dyslipidemia. Modulating-lipidemic effects of isosteviol might be
related to the potential enhancement of liver PPARα mRNA expression.

Introduction
The metabolic syndrome is a cluster of metabolic disorders, such
as abdominal obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension and impaired fasting glucose tolerance (insulin resistance). Type 2 diabetes mellitus
is characterized by a progressive decline in insulin action with relative glucagon excess, followed by the inability of β-cells to compensate for insulin resistance: a characteristic metabolic defect that
precedes overt β-cell dysfunction and is associated with resistance
to insulin-mediated glucose disposal at the periphery and compensatory hyperinsulinemia. The β-cells normally compensate for insulin
resistance by secreting increasing amounts of insulin to maintain glucose homeostasis. During the progress of the pathogenesis, however,
this β-cell function becomes impaired leading to deterioration in glucose homeostasis and subsequent development of impaired glucose
tolerance and diabetes (Lebovitz and Banerji, 2004; Saltiel and
Olefsky, 1996). Increased free fatty acids in serum are mediators of

predisposition, aging, obesity, poor diet and a sedentary lifestyle are
major risk factors involved in the development of type 2 diabetes
(McIntosh and Pederson, 1999; Ramarao and Kaul, 1999).
Stevia rebaudiana is a shrub native to Brazil and Paraguay. Extracts
from S. rebaudiana have been used for many years in South America in
the treatment of diabetes (Soejarto et al., 1982). Stevioside and its
metabolic product, steviol, were shown to stimulate glucosedependent insulin secretion from islet cells in vitro. Steviol is more
potent than stevioside (Jeppesen et al., 2000) and is able to exert a
hypoglycemic and hypotensive effect on the diabetic GK rat
(Jeppesen et al., 2003). However, application of stevioside is limited
due to its low oral bioavailability and its metabolite, steviol, having
mutagenic properties (WHO, 1999). Pezzuto et al. (1985) investigated the mutagenicity of steviol and several related compounds and
found that while steviol was toxic and mutagenic, while other related
compounds tested including isosteviol, ent-kaurenoic acid, steviol16a, 17-epoxide and dihydrosteviol A&B did not possess mutagenic
properties (Pezzuto et al., 1985). Isosteviol (ent-16-ketobeyeran-19oic acid, Fig. 1) is an acid hydrolysate of stevioside. We have reported
that isosteviol can alleviate the injury induced by ischemia–reperfusion

in isolated perfused guinea pig heart (Xu et al., 2007b), rat heart in vivo
(Xu et al., 2007a) and rat brain in vivo (Xu et al., 2008). We also found
that isosteviol was able to reduce plasma glucose concentrations but
did not have an impact on plasma insulin levels during an intravenous
glucose tolerance test in Zucker diabetic fatty rats (Ma et al., 2007). Recently, Nordentoft et al. reported that isosteviol can improve glucose
homeostasis, insulin sensitivity and the lipid proﬁle, and up-regulate
the expression of several key β-cell genes, including insulin regulatory
transcription factors in islets of the diabetic KKAy mouse (Nordentoft
et al., 2008). In rodent studies, isosteviol has an LD50 of over 500 mg/
kg in rats and over 600 mg/kg in mice when administered intravenously. These doses increase by 40% and 80% respectively when isosteviol is
administered i.p. The maximum tolerated oral dose is 3.16 g/kg in rats
and 5.06 g/kg in mice. Autopsy reveals distension of major blood vessels
as a possible cause of death (Xu et al., 1994). An LD50 of over 500 mg/kg
allows a good level of safety when compared to the doses between 0.2
and 10 mg/kg used in the studies described above, suggesting a therapeutic ratio in the order of 100.
In the present study, high-fat emulsion fed rats were selected as
the animal model to study the effects of isosteviol on lipotoxicity by
measuring fasting serum glucose (FSG), fasting serum insulin (FSI),
intravenous glucose tolerance test (IVGTT), serum total cholesterol
(TC), triglyceride (TG), high density lipoprotein (HDL) and low density lipoprotein (LDL). Rationality of the animal model is supported by a
range of previous studies, demonstrating that high-fat diet feeding
can cause impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and Type 2 diabetes in rodents, and can affect the respiratory capacity, ROS generation, fatty
acid β-oxidation, mitochondrial ADP/ATP translocator inhibition,
and regulation of kinases involved in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism (Ciapaite et al., 2007; Gustafson et al., 2002; Holness et al., 2003;
Raffaella et al., 2008). In particular, Raffaella et al. (2008) reported
that adult rats fed with a high-fat diet for 7 weeks exhibited obesity,
insulin resistance, hepatic steatosis, reduced respiratory capacity
and increased oxidative stress in liver mitochondria.
Material and methods

31

standard pellet diet (Anlimo Co., Nanjing) and water ad libitum. The
HFE rats were administered high fat emulsion 10 mL/kg once per day
(after fasting 4 h from 10.00 am) for two weeks. This high-fat emulsion
was administrated via oral gavage in order to overcome natural aversion to the high-fat diet due to its taste.
The high-fat emulsion (100 mL) consisted of lard 40 g, cholesterol
5 g, swine bile acid salt 2 g, glycerol 10 mL, propylthiouracil 1 g, vitamin mixture and distilled water. This emulsion was stored at 4 °C,
then heated in a 45 °C water bath and fully mixed before use. The
fasting (16 h) serum glucose of HFE rats were assayed after 14 days
of feeding and rats with FSG ≥11.1 mol/L selected for further pharmacological studies.
Before oral administration of drugs, the rats were anesthetized by
pentobarbital 30 mg/kg i.p. A midline incision in the frontal part of
the neck was made and the right extra-jugular vein was isolated. A
PE-50 polyethylene tube was inserted 30 mm into the vein and held
in position by ligatures. The free end of the catheter was exteriorized
at the neck leaving 2.5 cm of the catheter outside the animal. The
catheter was ﬁlled with 0.9% saline containing 10 U/mL heparin and
closed with a ﬁshing line inserted into the lumen. Animals were
caged individually with free access to food and water. The catheters
were ﬂushed daily with 0.2 mL saline/heparin to keep them open.
The animals were allowed to recover for 6 days after the operation.
Chemicals
Stevioside was purchased from Stevioside Sweetener Factory, Nankai
University (Tianjin, China). Isosteviol was produced by the acidic hydrolysis of stevioside according to procedures previously described in the
literature (Avent et al., 1990). The chemical structure of the yielded
product was conﬁrmed by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy,
infrared spectroscopy and determination of melting point (212 °C).
The purity of the isosteviol (99%) was determined by HPLC. Rosiglitazone maleate was a gift from Aosaikang Pharmaceutical Company
(Nanjing, China). The compounds were administered orally as the suspension solution by mixing with vehicle 0.1% sodium carboxyl methyl
cellulose (Na-CMC) and 0.9% sodium chloride solution.
Other agents including palmitate, cholesterol, swine bile acid salt,
glycerol and propylthiouracil were obtained from commercial sources.
Assays for glycemia, serum insulin and lipidemia
Rats were lightly anesthetized with ether. Blood (1.0 mL) for measuring the levels of FSG, FSI and serum lipids was collected from the right
jugular vein into Eppendorf tubes containing heparin (20 μL, 200 IU/
mL). The plasma was separated by centrifugation, 6308 ×g for 10 min
and was analyzed for glucose (GPO-POD method). The remaining plasma
samples were then stored at − 20 °C until the insulin determination
was made using a [ 125I] insulin radioimmunoassay kit (Kelmei Biotech
Co., Beijing).
The serum TC (CHOD-PAP method), TG (POD-PAP method), HDL
(PTA-Mg2 + method) and LDL-cholesterol (PVC sedimentation method)
were assayed with commercially available colorimetric diagnostic kits.

Animals
Experimental procedures
The study was conducted according to the Guidelines for the Care
and Use of Experimental Animals and approved by the Institute of
Medical Experimental Animal Ethics Committee, Southeast University.
Male Sprague–Dawley rats (age 7–8 weeks, 230 ± 20 g) were supplied
by the Experimental Animal Center, Southeast University. The rats
were housed in plastic cages, 4 rats per cage in a room with a 12/12 h
light/dark cycle, ambient temperature of 22 to 25 °C and 65 ± 5%
humidity. Before the experimental intervention, all rats were habituated to the new environment for one week. The rats were divided
into a normal control group (NC) and a high-fat emulsion-fed model
group (HFE). All rats were provided with commercial rat normal

Intravenous glucose tolerance test (IVGTT)
The last dose of drug was orally administrated after 8 h fasting
(water ad libitum). An intravenous catheter was connected to a polyethylene tube system (PE50) for taking blood samples 15.5 h after the
commencement of fasting. Thirty minutes later, the t = 0 blood sample was collected. Then D-glucose (1.0 g/kg, 2 mL/kg) was administered by penal vein as a bolus injection over 20 s. Blood samples
(0.2 mL) were drawn into chilled tubes containing heparin at t = 5,
15, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min. The samples were then centrifuged
(4 °C, 6308 ×g, 10 min) and the plasma was frozen for subsequent
analysis of insulin and glucose. Blood was replaced by isotonic saline
to avoid volume depletion.

Effects of isosteviol on palmitate supplemented HFE rats
Another group of rats were gavaged with high-fat emulsion supplemented with 10% palmitate for 14 days, followed by oral administration with isosteviol 0.2 to 5.0 mg/kg or RSG for 7 consecutive days.
Assays of FSG, FSI, serum lipids and IVGTT were performed. In addition, effects of isosteviol on HFE rats and palmitate supplemented
HFE rats were compared to investigate the inﬂuence of the supplementation of palmitate on the hypoglycemic and lipid modulating
effects of isosteviol.

Ultrastructure of pancreas
Small fragments of the pancreas (1 mm 3) were ﬁxed in Karnowsky's ﬁxative for 3 h at room temperature. Following several washes
with aqueous 0.2 M sucrose plus 0.1 M NaCl solution, the tissues
were post-ﬁxed in 1% OsO4 for 1 h at 4 °C. They were then washed
with aqueous 0.2 M sucrose plus 0.1 M NaCl solution and dehydrated
using a graded ethanol series and absolute acetone solutions. After
that, they were immersed for 4 h at room temperature in acetone:
epoxy resin (1:1) mixture and embedded in pure resin (Epon 812).
Semi-thin sections (0.5 mm) were cut to localize islets within the
pancreas fragments before ultrathin sections (70 nm) were obtained
and transferred to copper grids (200 mesh). The ultrathin sections
were stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate and observed by
transmission electron microscopy.

represented as insulin resistance according to the homoeostatic

Intravenous glucose tolerance test (IVGTT)
A single intravenous bolus administration with isosteviol in normal rats
There were no differences in the pre-drug values of serum glucose
and insulin between treatment groups. In the IVGTT, isosteviol (0.2 to
5 mg/kg) had no effect on serum glucose or insulin concentrations at
any time point, k value, IAUC0–30 min or IAUC0–120 min over the
120 min of IVGTT (Fig. 3).
Chronic treatment with isosteviol for 7 days in normal rats
As seen with a single i.v. administration, oral gavage of isosteviol
for 7 days had no effect on the results from IVGTT in normal rats
(Fig. 4).
Chronic treatment with isosteviol in HFE rats
The serum glucose levels in MC rats were consistently higher than
for control rats throughout the IVGTT, which is reﬂected in the k
value, IAUC30 min (glucose) and IAUC120 min (glucose) (Fig. 5). Isosteviol
(0.2 and 1.0 mg/kg) and rosiglitazone treated rats had signiﬁcantly
improved glucose levels in the IVGTT, but this effect was not seen in
isosteviol 5.0 mg/kg/day group.
The serum insulin increased rapidly after glucose-loading, the
glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) in HFE rats was not as
pronounced as that in normal rats. There were no signiﬁcant difference in GSIS between drug-treated groups and MC group, although
the values of isosteviol groups were slightly lower than those of the
model control group (Fig. 5B).
Effects of isosteviol on serum lipids

Discussion
Obese individuals are at much greater risk of developing type 2
diabetes and cardiovascular disease and it has been suggested that
ectopic fat is a link between obesity and these diseases (Roger
et al., 2004; Wilson Peter et al., 2002). In obesity, lipid droplets accumulate in the cytoplasm of cells in tissues such as the liver, muscle,
heart and pancreas, and an excessive accumulation of these lipids
may lead to cell dysfunction or cell death: a phenomenon known as
lipotoxicity. The term lipotoxicity was ﬁrst used in the context of
fat-induced insulin resistance (IR) and impaired glucose-stimulated
insulin secretion (GSIS) leading to type II diabetes (Unger, 1995).
Type II diabetes has two main pathophysiological features: (1) IR in
several tissues, especially in liver and muscle; and (2) impaired GSIS
in the pancreatic β-cells (DeFronzo et al., 1979). The data from human
and animal studies shows that ectopic lipid accumulation is associated
with insulin resistance in muscle and liver, and with functional losses
in the pancreas and the heart in animal models (Van Herpen and
Schrauwen-Hinderling, 2008).
In our experiment, normal SD rats were forced to intake high-fat
emulsion for 14 days. The main components of the fat emulsion included lard, bile acid salt to enhance the absorption of fatty acid in
the intestine; propylthiouracil which is a inhibitor of thyroid hormones
synthesis, T4 to T3 transformation, and cholesterol. This diet resulted
in an animal model with insulin deﬁciency, hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia. Post-drug FSG, FSI and IRI were lower signiﬁcantly in
isosteviol-treated rats compared to the MC group, suggesting that
the hyperglycemia induced by HFE is ameliorated by chronic treatment
with isosteviol and RSG.

As previously reported, chronic oral treatment (6 weeks) with isosteviol (20 mg/kg/day) improves glucose homeostasis, increases insulin sensitivity, lowers plasma triglycerides and lowers weight in
diabetic KKAy mice. Isosteviol markedly changes the gene expression
proﬁle of the key insulin regulatory genes GLUT2, Ins1, Ins2, Pdx1/Ipf1,
β2/Neurod1, Pax6 and 11-β-HSD-1 and β-cell transcription factors
Nkx2-2, Nkx6-1, C/EBPalpha and FoxA2 in isolated islets of the KKAy
mice (Nordentoft et al., 2008). In this experiment the increase in levels
of TC, TG and LDL was shown in the rats fed with HFE, and the signs
became more pronounced after continuous gavage with HFE for
7 days in the model control group. The lipid-modulating effects of
isosteviol, including decrease in TC and LDL and increase in HDL,
were demonstrated in HFE rats, although the decrease in serum TG
by isosteviol observed in KKAy mice did not occur in our experiment.
This difference could be due to the differences in species, model type
or duration of drug administration.
The intravenous glucose tolerance test (IVGTT) is a commonly used
technique to measure acute, ﬁrst-phase insulin release in response to
a glucose load and therefore represents a useful method to assess
pancreatic function (Cobelli et al., 2007). Although there was increase
in insulin release when stimulated by glucose, this did not affect
serum glucose suggesting that there was insulin resistance in HFE
model control group. In contrast, there was no marked increase in
serum insulin in HFE rats administrated with isosteviol orally at doses
of 0.2 and 1.0 mg/kg/day and the decrease in serum glucose was similar
to normal control rats.
The IAUCglucose of the isosteviol 0.2 and 1.0 mg/kg/day groups was
lower than the MC group, and the k values of serum glucose disappearance rate were higher in isosteviol-treated groups compared to
the MC group, even though there were no signiﬁcant differences in
IAUCinsulin between the isosteviol and MC groups. This indicates that
the hypoglycemic effects of isosteviol result from an increase in


D. Xu et al. / Life Sciences 90 (2012) 30–38

glucose utilization in peripheral tissue and amelioration of insulin
resistance. In ZDF rats, isosteviol at 5 and 10 mg/kg caused a signiﬁcant reduction in the AUC of glucose over the IVGTT period and did
not increase plasma insulin level (Ma et al., 2007). These are in line
with the results obtained from this experiment. Together these results
strongly suggest that enhancing insulin release does not contribute
to the hypoglycemic effects of isosteviol, despite the increase in insulin release being demonstrated in vitro (Nordentoft et al., 2008).
Furthermore, the proﬁles of basal FSG, IVGTT and lipids were unaffected either by isosteviol 0.2 to 5.0 mg/kg/day i.e. for 7 days or a single
bolus intravenous administration at the same dose in normal rats,
suggesting that the level of normal serum glucose is not affected by
isosteviol at these doses, and the hypoglycemic effects of isosteviol
are dependent on the level of serum glucose.
Palmitate is a free fatty acid (FFA) that is known to alter β-cell
gene expression and cause toxicity even when moderately elevated
(El-Assaad et al., 2003; Kelpe Cynthia et al., 2003; Maedler et al.,
2001, 2003; Ritz-Laser et al., 1999). Stevioside, the parent compound
of isosteviol, protects both α and β-cells against the effects of palmitate (Chen et al., 2006; Hong et al., 2006). Furthermore, Hong
et al. (2006) suggested that the presence of palmitate contributes
to stevioside's protective effects because in the presence of palmitate, stevioside enhances the gene expression of stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD). SCD converts palmitate to palmitoleate which is protective
against apoptosis. Within the current study, the effects of isosteviol
on serum glucose and lipids were attenuated by palmitate in the
HFE fed rats. This suggests that isosteviol exerts its protective effects
though a different mechanism to stevioside, which may be counteracted by the presence of palmitate.
The fasting serum insulin level, GSIS and the insulin granules of
β-cells were less in HFE rats compared with normal rats, suggesting
that the function of insulin secretion by β-cells was impaired in HFE
rats. The fatty acid-induced IR and impaired β-cell function may
stem from the abnormalities of insulin signaling pathways. Proinﬂammatory cytokines such as TNFα impair insulin action through
serine threonine phosphorylation of the insulin signaling pathways
(Hotamisligil, 2006). Key steps in the cytokine-induced proinﬂammatory cellular response are activation of NFκB and AP1 through
phosphorylation of IκKβ and JNK, respectively (Itani Samar et al.,
2002). Abnormal mitochondrial function has been implicated in IR
and impaired GSIS (Lowell and Shulman, 2005). Increased exposure
to long chain fatty acids leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired oxidative capacity. This occurs due to a reduced proton gradient, matrix swelling and enhanced production of ROS (Schrauwen,
2007). ROS produced during high mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation
and/or endoplasmic reticulum stress activates cellular inﬂammatory
pathways (JNK–AP1 and IκKβ–NκFB) leading to cellular inﬂammation and apoptosis (Kamata et al., 2005).
Under the electron microscope, the ectopic lipid accumulation and
absence of insulin granules in the pancreas demonstrates that the
function and structure of islet β-cells were affected in rats fed with
high fat emulsion for 21 days. Treatment with isosteviol attenuates
the lipid accumulation and obviously increases the insulin granules,
suggesting that protection of islet might be an important role of isosteviol's anti-hyperglycemia and anti-dyslipidemia activity.
To further investigate the mechanism of isosteviol's activity in
hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia, we checked the expression of hepatic PPARα mRNA in the HFE-rats as PPARα regulates the expression
of numerous genes involved in lipid uptake, catabolism and homeostasis in many tissues including the liver (Peters et al., 1997). PPARs are
activated by a wide range of fatty acids and hypolipidemic drugs,
such as cloﬁbrate, that lower triglyceride levels in man (Green, 1995).
In addition, pancreatic islet response to hyperglycemia is dependent
on PPARα (Bihan et al., 2005; Schoonjans et al., 1996). The activation
of PPARs can reduce lipotoxicity. This occurs through induction of
mitochondrial biogenesis, increased fatty acid oxidation, reduced

37

tissue accumulation of diacylglycerol and ceramides, down-regulation
of adaptor-related protein complex 1 and NFκB activation (Lalloyer
et al., 2006; Medina-Gomez et al., 2007). The increase in expression
hepatocyte PPARα mRNA in isosteviol-treated HFE rats in the current
work indicates that PPARα is involved in the modulating-lipid effects
of isosteviol.
It has been demonstrated that pretreatment with isosteviol enhances the expression of the antiapoptosis factor, Bcl-2, and inhibits
the expression of NF-κB and COX-2 (Xu et al., 2008). It also increases
SOD and GSH-PX activity and decreases MDA content of the myocardium induced by ischemia–reperfusion in anesthetized rats
(Xu et al., 2007a,b). Mizushina reported isosteviol causes a marked
reduction in TPA (12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate)-induced
inﬂammation (inhibitory effect, 53%) (Mizushina et al., 2005). It
is therefore possible that isosteviol's anti-inﬂammatory effect might
partly participate in its hypoglycemic and lipidemia modulating effects.
Conclusions
The hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia induced by gavage with highfat emulsion were attenuated by chronic treatment with isosteviol. The
underlying mechanism may be multiform, including anti-inﬂammation,
anti-oxidation, anti-apoptosis, activation of PPARα, and mitigating β-cell
damage induced by lipid. The modulating-lipidemic effects of isosteviol
may be the result of the potential enhancement of liver PPARα mRNA
expression.
